t: Maximum Total Value of Covered Indices
o:
Each token starting at index i may end up at any index j <= i (it moves left one step at a time, and each token moves at most once). Multiple tokens may stack, but only distinct occupied indices count. So the task is: choose a set T of indices maximizing sum of nums[j] for j in T, subject to a matching existing between T and the tokens where each chosen index j gets a token starting at some position >= j.

By Hall's theorem this matching exists iff for every k, the number of chosen indices in [k, n-1] does not exceed the number of tokens whose start lies in [k, n-1].

Example 1: tokens at 1 and 3; choosing {0, 2} works (token 1 -> 0, token 3 -> 2) giving 9 + 6 = 15. Choosing {1, 2} gives only 8. Example 2: the single token at 2 best stays put, answer 4. Example 3 shows why naive per-index greed fails: taking index 1 (value 3) wastes the token needed for index 0 (value 9).

With n up to 1e5, an O(n^2) DP is borderline but instructive; the intended solution is an O(n log n) greedy with a heap.
k: A token starting at i can cover ANY index j <= i, so the problem is choosing a subset of indices with a matching to tokens.
Feasibility (Hall's condition): for every k, #chosen indices >= k must be <= #tokens starting at >= k.
Process right to left, tentatively add each nums[i], and whenever the tentative selection violates the suffix-token budget, discard the smallest selected value via a min-heap.

a.n: Approach 1: Dynamic Programming over suffix budgets
a.i: Process indices from right to left. Let suf[i] be the number of tokens starting at positions >= i. Any valid selection restricted to [i, n-1] may contain at most suf[i] indices. Define dp[c] = maximum value achievable choosing exactly c indices among those processed so far. When adding index i, either skip it or extend a selection of size c-1 by nums[i], keeping only states with c <= suf[i]. The answer is the maximum dp value. This directly encodes Hall's condition and is easy to prove correct.
s: Compute suf[i] = number of '1' characters in s[i..n-1].
Initialize dp[0] = 0 and dp[c] = -infinity for c > 0.
Iterate i from n-1 down to 0; new_dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c-1] + nums[i]) for c from min(processed, suf[i]) down to 1.
Clamp state space: only sizes c <= suf[i] survive after processing index i.
a.t: O(n^2) — for each of n indices we scan up to n candidate selection sizes.
a.sp: O(n) — two DP arrays of length n+1 plus the suffix-count array.

a.i: Scan right to left maintaining a min-heap of currently selected values. When visiting index i, tentatively select it (push nums[i]), then enforce Hall's condition for k = i: the heap size must not exceed suf[i] (tokens starting at >= i). If it does, evict the smallest selected value — swapping a smaller value for the current larger one never hurts, and any selection satisfying all suffix budgets is feasible. All selected values that remain form the optimal set. This is the classic exchange-argument greedy for deadline-style matching problems.
s: Precompute suf[i] = number of tokens at positions >= i.
For i from n-1 down to 0: push nums[i] into the heap.
While heap size > suf[i], pop the minimum (that value is permanently discarded).
Return the sum of remaining heap elements.
a.t: O(n log n) — each index is pushed once and popped at most once from the heap.
a.sp: O(n) — the heap and suffix-count array hold at most n elements.

w: In an interview, present the DP first to establish the matching/Hall's-condition framing, then optimize to the heap greedy — interviewers love seeing the exchange argument (evicting the smallest selected value when a suffix budget is exceeded is never worse). Common pitfalls: (1) assuming a simple per-index greedy works — Example 3 disproves it; (2) forgetting tokens can stack on one index but only distinct indices count; (3) off-by-one in the suffix budget (use suf[i], tokens at positions >= i, checked right after adding index i). Edge cases: all zeros in s (answer 0), single element, all ones in s (answer is sum of all nums). Follow-ups: what if tokens could also move right, or if each token had a limited move distance d (then suf becomes a sliding-window count and the same heap idea applies); returning the actual assignment of tokens to indices.
